blocks.text: "A PROPHETESS, THE WIFE OF LAPIDOTH", WHO JUDGED ISRAEL (JUDGES 4:4) · THE JUDGES
Deborah. Gave Barak the LORD’s command and the day of battle, and sang the victory.
"She judged Israel at that time": she sat under the palm tree of Deborah between Ramah and Beth-el, "and the children of Israel came up to her for judgment".
"She judged Israel at that time": she sat under the palm tree of Deborah between Ramah and Beth-el, "and the children of Israel came up to her for judgment". Judges 4:4–5
She gave the LORD’s command to Barak as a question: "Hath not the LORD God of Israel commanded, saying, Go and draw toward mount Tabor". Judges 4:6

The victory is told twice, in prose and in a song: "Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day". In the song she is called on: "Awake, awake, Deborah: awake, awake, utter a song". Judges 5:1 Judges 5:12
“And I will draw unto thee to the river Kishon Sisera, the captain of Jabin’s army, with his chariots and his multitude; and I will deliver him into thine hand.”
The word in its main themes
“Hath not the LORD God of Israel commanded, saying, Go and draw toward mount Tabor, and take with thee ten thousand men of the children of Naphtali and of the children of Zebulun?”
“Up; for this is the day in which the LORD hath delivered Sisera into thine hand: is not the LORD gone out before thee?”
The song: the LORD came from Seir
“LORD, when thou wentest out of Seir, when thou marchedst out of the field of Edom, the earth trembled, and the heavens dropped, the clouds also dropped water.”
“So let all thine enemies perish, O LORD: but let them that love him be as the sun when he goeth forth in his might.”
Those who came and those who stayed
“Curse ye Meroz, said the angel of the LORD, curse ye bitterly the inhabitants thereof; because they came not to the help of the LORD”
To whom the word was spoken
“I will surely go with thee: notwithstanding the journey that thou takest shall not be for thine honour; for the LORD shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman.”
“Up; for this is the day in which the LORD hath delivered Sisera into thine hand”
“Hear, O ye kings; give ear, O ye princes; I, even I, will sing unto the LORD”
“Curse ye Meroz, said the angel of the LORD, curse ye bitterly the inhabitants thereof”
Who stood with her, and against her
Judges ends her story with the song and the words "And the land had rest forty years"; it does not record her death. Judges 5:31
Keil (1872); "the great majority of scholars", such as Ewald, Hitzig and Renan, as reported by Moore (1895)
Keil holds that verse 1 means the song was sung by Deborah and Barak together, not made by both, and that "the poetess or writer of the song, according to vers. 3, 7, and 12, was Deborah."[13]
A poet of the time, not Deborah
Moore (1895); also Wellhausen, Reuss, Graetz, Kuenen and others, as listed by Moore

Moore notes that some ancient versions read verse 7 in the third person, "until Deborah arose", and that the Hebrew "may equally well be rendered, until thou didst arise, Deborah"; verse 12 calls on her, and elsewhere the song speaks of her in the third person. He calls it "the natural and almost necessary inference" that "Deborah herself is not the author", and thinks it more probable "that the poem was made by one under the immediate inspiration of the events". He calls it "the oldest extant monument of Hebrew literature".[14]
Maurice Vernes (1883–1892), as reported by Moore (1895)

Moore reports that Vernes put the prose account no earlier than the 5th century BC and the song a century or more later, and called it an artificial work. Moore answers that Vernes’ facts, where accurate, "do not justify his conclusions".[14]
Judges gives no account of how the word first came to Deborah, and does not name her tribe.

Judges 4:9 says the LORD would sell Sisera "into the hand of a woman", and 4:21–22 tells how Jael killed him; the text sets the two side by side but does not say in so many words that the word came to pass.
Scripture does not record her death. Hebrews 11:32 names Barak, not Deborah.
